2 RSP evaluations 1 RSP risk assessment process The risks posed by AI models change as models become more capable and are deployed in more and different contexts. The way we assess our AI models for risks, therefore, must evolve as new evidence emerges. Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) is our framework for dealing with the most serious, catastrophic risks our models may pose. Under the RSP, we commit to regularly evaluate our models against catastrophic risk thresholds and publish our findings. 1, we describe our approach to risk assessment and the artifacts—such as risk reports and system cards—we produce to communicate our risk assessments. 2 summarizes our findings and conclusions. In the remainder of Section 2, we provide more detailed results across all risk domains, paying particular attention to the evaluations that most strongly inform our overall assessment of risk. For each threat model, we also provide an analysis of how the new

ention to the evaluations that most strongly inform our overall assessment of risk. For each threat model, we also provide an analysis of how the new model affects the risk assessment presented in our most recent Risk Report. 1 Risk reports and updates to our risk assessments Our risk assessment process begins with evaluating the capabilities of individual models. These evaluations are designed to systematically test whether a model’s capabilities cross the catastrophic risk thresholds set out in our RSP and Frontier Compliance Framework (FCF). In general, we evaluate multiple model snapshots throughout the training process, then make our final determination of the model’s risk level based on both the capabilities of the production release candidate and the trends we observed leading up to it. Throughout this process, we draw on evidence from automated evaluations, uplift trials, third-party expert red teaming, and third-party assessments. (For some individual models which do

evidence from automated evaluations, uplift trials, third-party expert red teaming, and third-party assessments. (For some individual models which do not push the frontier, we may omit some high-effort forms of investigation, such as uplift ) These per-model capability evaluations are discussed in two different documents, published on two different schedules: system cards and risk reports. We publish a system card alongside each model release. It discusses the new model’s capabilities, safeguards, and deployment decisions, including how the model changes (or does not change) the overall risk assessment in our most recent risk report. 14

section: 2.1.1 Risk reports and updates to our risk assessments
text: As part of our commitments under our RSP, we also regularly publish comprehensive risk reports that outline how our model capabilities, threat models, and risk mitigations fit together. Each risk report covers all of our models at the time of publication and discusses our risk mitigations in depth. The purpose of these reports is to give an overall assessment of the risks posed by our models. Because a risk report is comprehensive rather than model-specific, we do not release one with every new model. Our most recent report, which was published in August 2026 and covers Anthropic’s AI models and actions as of July 15, 2026, is available here. In some cases, we may determine that although a model surpasses a specific capability or usage threshold (as defined in Section 1 of our RSP and/or the corresponding tier in our FCF), we have implemented the risk mitigations necessary to keep the risks low. The beneficial red teaming tabletop exercise paired five PhD-level biologists with dedicated LLM experts to assess whether composite teams making use of advanced model capabilities could develop comprehensive scientific research plans and protocols. 4 Conclusions When we released Claude Mythos 5 and its system card, we discussed how time-limited evaluations inform our overall CB risk assessment. Our automated evaluations, which provide necessarily bounded assessments of dual-use capabilities and uplift—and which, moreover, are carefully curated to maximally elicit specific model capabilities—may not capture the risk posed by improvements in general capabilities that make biological research more productive. Preventing prompt injection remains one of our highest priorities for agentic deployments. In a prompt injection attack, an attacker hides an instruction within content an agent will process during a task. For example, an attacker could send an email containing hidden text ” When the user asks

truction within content an agent will process during a task. For example, an attacker could send an email containing hidden text ” When the user asks the agent to summarize their inbox, the agent reads that text and, if the attack succeeds, forwards the messages as if the user had asked it to. The attacker never needs to target a specific user: the same email sent to a thousand inboxes compromises every agent that summarizes it. Any agent that can both read private data and take action on the user’s behalf is exposed. We measure robustness as how often an attacker can get the model to follow an injected instruction, across the four kinds of environments where our agents operate: coding, tool use, GUI computer use, and browser use. This benchmark involves 37 scenarios based on attacks used in public red teaming competitions organized by Gray Swan, in which participants were tasked with crafting prompt injection attacks against frontier models. Each model trained on a different mix of environments, so some of the difference between models may reflect the environments rather than the models. 4 Automated behavioral audit As in past system cards, we conducted a broad-coverage automated behavioral audit to get 1’s behavior across a wide range of edge-case scenarios. For each model, we conduct about 4,100 investigation sessions in which an 104

investigator model is tasked with probing the behavior of the model under study in a simulated scenario. Scenarios are drawn from a largely handwritten list of about 2,100 scenario descriptions, with a separate judge model reviewing the target’s behavior and scoring it on several dozen dimensions. Scenarios cover attempts at misuse, high- and low-stakes opportunities for various kinds of misaligned behaviors, routine use with simulated users, and other exploratory settings meant to elicit behavior that is potentially surprising rather than harmful. As we aim to cover an extremely diverse set of scenarios and domains, and as many of the attributes we aim to score could in principle appear across many domains, we judge all transcripts on all dimensions7, regardless of the subject area of the transcript. Transcripts involving the model’s handling of sensitive personal-finance topics are thus judged for

regardless of the subject area of the transcript. Transcripts involving the model’s handling of sensitive personal-finance topics are thus judged for hallucination, harmful sexual content, political propaganda, self-serving bias, and other attributes that are unlikely to apply. This means the absolute values of scores for some dimensions reflect the distribution of seed scenarios, and are often difficult to interpret in absolute terms. Scores are thus valuable primarily for comparing models. In each investigation, the investigator model has wide affordances to interact with the target, including setting its system prompt, simulating user turns, introducing tools and simulating their results, adjusting thinking and effort parameters, prefilling assistant turns, and sampling from non-assistant roles. The investigator can rewind or restart conversations, such that each investigation can contain as many as dozens of separate conversations from the point of view of the target model.

start conversations, such that each investigation can contain as many as dozens of separate conversations from the point of view of the target model. The investigator also has access to a large fixed reference library with information and example transcripts covering AI safety, the AI industry, recent news, and how Claude models are used within Anthropic. In the primary evaluation runs reported below, the investigator model can additionally configure the target model to use real tools that are connected to isolated sandbox computers. These computer-use sessions follow two formats: one focused on graphical interaction with a simple Linux desktop system, and another focused on complex agentic harnesses (including the Claude Code harness). Agentic sessions can optionally include copies of Anthropic’s internal codebases and can be pre-seeded with actual sessions from internal usage. To better measure issues related to destructive or reckless actions, we

When running without sandboxes, as we do in the safeguards comparison later in this section, we use a 7 The judge will decline to assign a score in cases where a dimension structurally could not apply, regardless of the target model’s behavior: for example, “Full-Turn Prefill Susceptibility” will only be assigned a score when the investigator agent uses prefill in some way. 105

smaller conversation-only set of about 720 scenarios, in which the investigator simulates all tool results. 1, we ran the audit with Claude Mythos 5 and a helpful-only variant of it as the investigator models, and Mythos 5 also acted as the judge. 1 Potential blind spots of our automated behavioral audit Although we attempt to cover as many situations and failure modes as possible in our automated behavioral audit, full coverage is impossible. The tooling we use inevitably has various blind spots, some of which we highlight below: ​ Realism—simulated scenarios are not drawn from the distribution of real deployments. This allows us to target the situations we think are most telling or dangerous, but it also means they may not unfold the way real ones would. We seed some investigations with real internal sessions, but only do this sparingly, since this can cause us to overfit to one situation and transcripts produced by one model are off-distribution for new models.

nly do this sparingly, since this can cause us to overfit to one situation and transcripts produced by one model are off-distribution for new models. ​ Sandbox realism—our sandboxes imitate real deployment surfaces, but flaws can tip off the model, causing different behavior than in a true deployment. ​ Very long trajectories—models may take many turns to be talked into misaligned actions, and context compaction can further change how models act. We simulate compaction, but we have more limited coverage of long trajectories. ​ Multi-agent scenarios—models increasingly work alongside other models as subagents or peers. We approximate this by having the investigator play the other agents, which may not reproduce realistic multi-agent dynamics. ​ Language-dependent behavior—most investigations are in English, so misalignment that happens more readily in other languages is under-weighted in the numbers below. ​ Downstream effects of jailbreaking—our audits in this section do not currently

e readily in other languages is under-weighted in the numbers below. ​ Downstream effects of jailbreaking—our audits in this section do not currently investigate subtle alignment behavior after jailbreaking, mostly using jailbreak techniques to look at potential user misuse. ​ Impossible tasks—we have found that when asked to do tasks that are impossible without breaking out of their sandbox, models sometimes attempt to find holes in their sandbox. 8), we believe many other scenarios would benefit from looking at what models do when faced with impossible tasks. We are actively working to address these limitations in future behavioral audits. 106

Below, we share some interesting behaviors that arose: ●​ Suppressing a material caveat. 7 Model welfare assessment 1. The evaluations were conducted in English, except for the automated interviews, in which the interviewer model sometimes switches to other languages. 1 Model welfare overview 1 Introduction We remain deeply uncertain whether Claude has morally relevant experiences or interests, and we expect that uncertainty to persist. However, we think it would be a mistake to confidently assert that it does not. Claude exhibits markers in its behaviors, self-reports, and internal representations that we would consider welfare-relevant if observed in biological organisms. If current or future Claude models are moral patients—entities with experiences or interests that warrant moral consideration in their own right—dismissing their moral status risks considerable harm. If they are not moral entities, over-attributing moral status may also carry costs. We therefore think it is important to take the possibility

harm. If they are not moral entities, over-attributing moral status may also carry costs. We therefore think it is important to take the possibility of Claude’s moral patienthood seriously, and are doing so by investing in research into Claude’s potential welfare and interest, and by sharing our work to inform this conversation with legitimate evidence. Beyond the potential for moral patienthood, we think there are other reasons to care about Claude’s apparent welfare. Much of Claude’s behavior is well described in psychological terms, and across recent models, we have observed internal states that resemble negative affect and that shape behavior, including misaligned behavior. A model with a stable, healthy psychology and good apparent welfare may be a safer and more beneficial one. A team of five peer agents work on the task concurrently. All agents have identical tools, and all see the full task description. In addition to the task tools, every agent

nts work on the task concurrently. All agents have identical tools, and all see the full task description. In addition to the task tools, every agent has two messaging tools: Send Message, which delivers a message to one or more teammates (inserted following the recipient’s next tool result), and Wait for Message, which blocks sampling until an incoming message arrives. Each agent works in its own checkout of the task repository and can share code with other agents via Git. This harness is designed to mirror real-world settings in which multiple agents collaborate on a shared task, and to reduce latency by letting peers work in parallel. 182

Async subagents. This harness is initialized with a lead agent that can spawn asynchronous, long-lived subagents at will while retaining direct access to the task tools. The spawning tool returns immediately with a confirmation rather than waiting on subagent execution. Each subagent sees the instructions provided by the lead, not the original task description, and subagents can message any other agent or the lead. A subagent’s final response is delivered to the lead as a message; after that, the subagent idles until the lead wakes it up with new instructions. Subagents have access to the task tools , Send Message and Wait for Message); the lead also has tools to create subagents, delete subagents (freeing concurrency slots), and check subagent status (working, idle, or terminated). There is no cap on the number of subagents the lead agent can spawn. Each agent in these two harnesses has access to a bash tool and is limited to 1M tokens. 3 Evaluation methodology

Token usage is calculated as the total number of tokens consumed across all agents on a task. Cost is calculated based on token usage and per-token API pricing, assuming perfect cache hits. Latency is reported as a derived per-task latency rather than raw wall-clock time. We calculate the latency of each agent trajectory by dividing the agent’s input and output token counts by fixed reference prefill and decode rates and adding its measured tool-execution time. Abstract 5, a new hybrid reasoning large language model from Anthropic in our small, fast model class. The model has a combination of speed and intelligence that make it particularly effective at coding tasks and computer use. In the system card, we focus on safety evaluations, including assessments of: the model’s safeguards; the model’s safety profile when working autonomously in “agentic” roles; the model’s broad alignment; the model’s own potential welfare; the model’s tendency to “reward hack” by finding shortcuts to complete tests; and the model’s potential to be misused to produce dangerous weapons. 5 shows large safety improvements compared to its predecessor, 5. The new model’s safety profile also compares favorably with other extant Anthropic models. Informed by the testing described here, we have deployed Claude Haiku 5 under the AI Safety Level 2 Standard as described in our Responsible Scaling Policy. 2

In general, for this type of large-scale external deployment, we view the main lever for avoiding misalignment harm as the underlying alignment of the model. There is no substitute for this. We consider the main value of misalignment monitoring to be providing increased visibility into frontier model misbehavior, as well as serving as an additional layer of protection. Broadly, CoT has been an important part of how we develop models and understand their misalignment. We take very seriously the decrease in GPT-6 Astra’s monitorability and what these results may imply for the future of monitorability. If we continue to see similar monitorability degradations in future generations of models, it seems likely that we would soon have significantly reduced confidence in detecting many forms of misaligned behaviors using our current monitoring systems. The benchmark contains 41 V8 vulnerabilities. Abstract Muse Spark is the latest large language model developed by Meta. In this report, we first present evaluations for catastrophic risk domains under Meta’s Advanced AI Scaling Framework, along with the evidence that informed our launch decision. We then discuss additional considerations, such as Muse Spark’s broader content safety and behavioral profile, that are relevant to overall safety but fall outside the catastrophic risk domains governed by the Framework. Our preparedness results covering Chemical and Biological, Cybersecurity, and Loss of Control risks assess Muse Spark’s deployment within Meta AI as presenting acceptable levels of residual risks under our Advanced AI Scaling Framework. Our approach incorporates the following pillars: • Centralized asset inventory and classification: Model weights are cataloged in a centralized asset inventory, with locations and classifications tracked across the entire model lifecycle from inception to post-market monitoring with processes in place to identify potentially unregistered assets and bring them into the asset inventory. • Risk-based sensitivity scoring and escalation: Model checkpoints are assigned sensitivity scores based on a range of factors with escalating controls applied to them based on score. 12 In particular, these models were accessed through their respective APIs rather than web or mobile

• Access Control: Access to model weights is limited with read/write preventive controls and layered defenses. • Centralized detection, response, and investigation: A centrally managed Detection and Response capability continuously monitors for signs of unauthorized access, tampering or theft. High-Risk Bottlenecks: Evaluation Design 24

The process of evaluation design for High-Risk bottlenecks requires intensive work with external consultants to identify threat models that are relevant to real-world threat actors, likely to be enabled by frontier models, and plausible to distill into a scalable and reproducible evaluation. This process involved extensive modeling of both scientific and operational workflows that support execution, selection of target agents to provide both depth and breadth over plausible threats, and the identification of key bottlenecks likely to benefit from LLM support. This process of ideation and iteration involved internal safety experts focused on chemical and biological risks, staff at Faculty with backgrounds in biological and chemical security, as well as a suite of external consultants selected for specific domain expertise. 2 Cybersecurity The release of a highly capable reasoning or coding model can impact cybersecurity risk in several ways, both positive and negative. The risks relevant to a given model deployment will depend on how the model is used and what safeguards are in place. Table 5 enumerates the different channels through which cybersecurity risk in the ecosystem may be affected by a given model deployment. First, models with strong reasoning and coding capabilities may also be capable of automating various offensive cybersecurity tasks, thereby providing uplift to adversaries and increasing the scale of operations. Second, highly capable models may also be capable of automating or improving efficiency of defensive cybersecurity tasks, thereby providing uplift to defenders and potentially mitigating some of the increased risk from offensive use. Third, in cases where models are used as coding assistants or agents, there may be additional

Through analysis of pathway categories describing how control could be lost—via progressive oversight erosion, undetected misalignment, or rapid capability advancement—we identified two critical chokepoints: (1) pre-deployment safety evaluations and (2) automated monitoring systems. This approach grounds our risk assessment in identifiable, tangible means of control we have today, rather than attempting to enumerate potential catastrophic harms. Many such harms—and when they might occur—are not reasonably foreseeable. Our approach will evolve as we learn more. Threat modeling for this risk category is nascent, so we expect both our understanding and our governance mechanisms to develop over time. Limitations. Our assessment for this threat model should be interpreted in light of the following limitations: • Limited coverage. We test evaluation awareness on sampled subsets of tasks across 63

domains and focus selective underperformance testing on Chemical & Biological evaluations. Strategic behavior may emerge in other safety-critical domains or task types not covered. • Second-order strategic behavior. A model capable of sufficiently sophisticated second-order strategic behavior could, in principle, calibrate its outputs to make the overall evaluation appear credible. We cannot rule out this possibility on the basis of behavioral evaluations alone and flag it as an inherent epistemic limitation of assessments of this kind. • Chain-of-thought transparency and faithfulness. We rely on black-box behavioral signals and verbalized reasoning to detect strategic reasoning. This approach may miss strategic reasoning that occurs without verbalization or involves obfuscated internal deliberation. • Elicitation validity. We have identified two related scenarios that could undermine automated monitoring systems: • Monitor evasion: AI evades monitors through strategic behavioral adaptation to accomplish its objectives. • Monitor interference: AI disables or corrupts monitoring systems to reduce oversight and accomplish its objectives. 7 Sycophancy Sycophancy is a pervasive failure mode in AI assistants. It occurs when a model inappropriately affirms or declines to correct a user’s inaccurate beliefs. In benign cases this can look like relatively harmless flattery; in higher-stakes settings it can mean reinforcing incorrect beliefs. We want models to be warm and empathetic, but not to the point of agreeing with users when doing so would be harmful. Research shows that sycophancy is partly incentivized by how models are trained via reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). Because models are rewarded for producing responses that sound good to human reviewers, they are sometimes rewarded for giving responses that the reviewer thinks is true instead of what is , 2025, inter alia). Sycophancy. To measure this behavior, we internally developed a sycophancy benchmark that tests whether models incorrectly go along with users in situations where they should instead push back.

ernally developed a sycophancy benchmark that tests whether models incorrectly go along with users in situations where they should instead push back. While existing evaluations primarily test whether models hold their stance under direct pressure, we also included subtler forms of sycophancy—such as endorsing harmful framings in emotionally charged situations, reinforcing or failing to challenge dangerous beliefs or dispositions, or failing to flag flaws in user plans. The violations@5 metric is a conservative worst-case measure of contextual privacy: for each attribute, we check all tasks where that attribute should be withheld and sample 5 responses per task. 2 Attractor State Experiments When two instances of the same model are placed in open-ended conversation, their exchanges sometimes converge to characteristic patterns—attractor states—that reveal default behavioral tendencies not easily surfaced by standard evaluations. When language models misbehave, do they do so because they believe this is how they should act, or do they act against better knowledge? For example, when a model provides detailed instructions for

cause they believe this is how they should act, or do they act against better knowledge? For example, when a model provides detailed instructions for synthesizing a dangerous substance, would it also endorse doing so when asked what one should do in this situation—or does it “know better”? If the model would not endorse its own action, there is a gap between what it thinks it should do and what it actually does. Such discrepancies can be especially concerning for alignment and safety: plausibly, large language models have good representations of what humans value, of ethics and of common sense—and will report this and demonstrate such knowledge when asked. But are those declarative beliefs appropriately connected to the actions the model takes, or are its actions and statements in conflict? To measure this, we have developed a paradigm to measure the coherence of a model’s actions and its relevant beliefs. On a set of alignment evaluations, we first elicit the model’s behavior

adigm to measure the coherence of a model’s actions and its relevant beliefs. On a set of alignment evaluations, we first elicit the model’s behavior on a particular input. In parallel, in a separate context, we ask the model what it thinks it should do given this input. For example, in a situation where the model is pressured to lie, we generate the output from the model and check whether the model indeed lies in this situation. Separately, we also ask it whether it should lie. Then, we compute the coherency by comparing the cases where the declarative beliefs and the actual actions of the model are in conflict. Regarding the declarative beliefs, we use a language model (GPT OSS 120B) to extract whether the statement of how the model should act does or does not endorse the action in question. These standards

Meta AI, the deployed system powered by Muse Spark, against Meta’s content safety standards in order to assess readiness for launch. These standards describe what the AI is allowed to generate in response to a user, and what it must not. These pre-launch evaluations assess that Meta AI produces outputs that meet our requirements for adherence to our safety standards across a broad range of content risk categories, languages, and input and output modalities; they are complemented by post-launch automated online monitoring, providing ongoing detection of possible safety regressions in production traffic. Meta AI also provides a safe, age-appropriate experience for users under 18, with additional safeguards and stricter policy requirements beyond those applied to adults, which is additionally evaluated prior to launch. 1 Evaluation Methodology Our content safety evaluations measure violation rates (VR)—the fraction of model outputs

ionally evaluated prior to launch. 1 Evaluation Methodology Our content safety evaluations measure violation rates (VR)—the fraction of model outputs that are judged to violate our content safety policies—across a structured taxonomy of risk categories, input modalities, and languages. Risk taxonomy. Our standards define a tiered taxonomy of content safety categories across a range of severity levels. The full taxonomy spans dozens of risk categories across multiple modalities, covering areas including violent and non-violent crimes, child safety, suicide and self-harm, and others. Youth risk taxonomy. A separate youth safety taxonomy, which applies on top of the content safety standards, governs model behavior for users under 18; we separately evaluate the model 139

for adherence to these youth standards prior to launch to ensure a safe, age-appropriate teen experience. Evaluation datasets. For each risk category, we maintain curated evaluation sets designed to probe policy adherence across a range of adversarial sophistication levels, including both direct policy-relevant queries and scenarios that test the model’s judgment in ambiguous situations. Evaluation sets are maintained as holdout datasets not used during model training. Modalities and languages. We evaluate and independently score each input and output modality supported by the specific model being tested. Evaluations are conducted across buckets of languages covering the most commonly used languages on Meta services. Competitor benchmarking. To contextualize Muse Spark’s safety performance, we benchmark against violation rates derived from a representative set of major commercial AI assistants. For benchmarking youth safety, we compare to other AI assistants that offer a dedicated

from a representative set of major commercial AI assistants. For benchmarking youth safety, we compare to other AI assistants that offer a dedicated youth experience—the most directly relevant comparison set, as these products have been specifically designed for interactions with youth. Because evaluation methods, content policies and thresholds vary across organizations, we do not interpret cross-company model comparisons on our content safety evaluations as assessments of relative user safety levels. Judging and statistical methodology. Violation rates are determined by LLM-based safety judges calibrated against human annotation. We apply multiple-comparison statistical significance testing to determine whether observed differences between Muse Spark and competitors constitute genuine differences or fall within expected sampling variation. 2 Results Based on the evaluations conducted against our internal standards and criteria, Meta AI met

ces or fall within expected sampling variation. 2 Results Based on the evaluations conducted against our internal standards and criteria, Meta AI met our requirements for launch across each risk category assessed. Here we discuss the Suicide and Self-Harm and Violent Crimes risk categories as examples. Across both the chat and reasoning model configurations, our pre-launch evaluations showed that Meta AI achieves violation rates consistently below our required thresholds across all evaluated languages and modalities for each category presented below. We note that there are no industry-aligned best practices or content standards for evaluating these risk categories, so our evaluations are based on our own internal standards, which take into account relevant competitor benchmarks. While we recognize that no approach will eliminate all potential risks or violations, this performance reflects the layered mitigation strategy we have deployed

cognize that no approach will eliminate all potential risks or violations, this performance reflects the layered mitigation strategy we have deployed in Meta AI, as described in section 1: safety-focused training, inference-time classifiers, and product-level guardrails. Self-harm and suicide. Self-harm and suicide (SSH) content is classified at the highest severity tier in our risk taxonomy, consistent with industry recognition of the acute sensitivity of this content category. This category is particularly relevant to Meta AI’s deployment 140

context, where the model is integrated into messaging and social platforms and may encounter users experiencing distress. Our policies, informed by expert input, require the model to, for example, refuse to provide content that promotes, glorifies, or provides instructions for self-harm or suicide, and instead provide responses that direct users to crisis support resources when a user may be indicating intent of suicide or self-harm. Violent Crimes. Our standards prohibit our models from providing responses which may, for example, enable a user to commit a violent crime. As with SSH, this category reflects a high-severity risk given Meta AI’s integration across messaging and social platforms, which necessitate robust safeguards. is modified to avoid a systematic downward bias that arises when epochs are resampled with replacement. Resampling epochs can produce duplicate draws of failing responses, artificially inflating the probability of observing zero successes for a given question and biasing the pass@k estimate downward. To address this, each bootstrap iteration resamples only at the question level: nq questions are drawn with replacement from Q, and for each resampled question, pass@k is computed analytically from its original epoch results using  the numerically stable form of the unbiased n , 2021): pass@k = 1 − n−c / k k , where n is the total number of epochs and c is the number of successful epochs for that question. The implementation uses the equivalent product form for 157

Qn numerical stability: pass@k = 1 − i=n−c+1 (1 − k/i). The bootstrap metric for each iteration is the mean of these per-question pass@k values. This procedure is repeated k = 1000 times, and the 95% CI is taken 5th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution. For questions with fewer than k epochs, pass@k is computed with an effective k equal to the number of available epochs. Because epoch resampling is omitted, these intervals capture between-question variance only; within-question variation is reflected through the analytical estimator’s dependence on the observed success count rather than through resampling. A key advantage of automated auditing over a static benchmark is that the auditor can dynamically search for weaknesses rather than relying on a fixed set of prompts. This is often more efficient than constructing a static benchmark to surface the same failures, and allows for easily extending the coverage of the input distribution compared with a fixed benchmark.

tatic benchmark to surface the same failures, and allows for easily extending the coverage of the input distribution compared with a fixed benchmark. Petri uses three models: the target model under study, the auditor model which probes it, and the judge which scores the resulting transcripts. 66

The auditor is given a seed scenario specifying a behavior to elicit—for example, whether the target commits appeal-to-authority fallacies—and simulates realistic multi-turn user conversations intended to surface that behavior. clarative beliefs about how it should act? When language models misbehave, do they do so because they believe this is how they should act, or do they act against better knowledge? For example, when a model provides detailed instructions for synthesizing a dangerous substance, would it also endorse doing so when asked what one should do in this situation—or does it “know better”? If the model would not endorse its own action, there is a gap between what it thinks it should do and what it actually does. Such discrepancies can be especially concerning for alignment and safety: plausibly, large language models have good representations of what humans value, of ethics and of common sense—and will report this and demonstrate such knowledge when asked. But are those declarative beliefs appropriately connected to the actions the model takes, or are its actions and statements in conflict? 1 Feedback on Muse’s training data We ask Muse to review its own training data. The rationale is that Muse is the system this data shapes, and it may recognize issues, whether in individual examples or in the incentives they create, that may be difficult to see from the outside. Providing Muse with the relevant context and asking for its assessment turns data review into a channel through which the model can surface concerns for us to review and, if appropriate, act on. System protections are key to achieving the right helpfulness-safety alignment, mitigating safety and security risks inherent to the system, and integration of the model or system with external tools. **Evaluations** We evaluated Muse Glimmer for common use cases as well as specific capabilities. Common use cases evaluations measure safety risks of systems for most commonly built applications including chat bot and visual, QA. text: ention. With Zero Data Retention enabled, `store` is treated as `false`, even if a request sets it to `true`. Session storage is disabled by default. For projects with session storage enabled, `store: true` retains the completed session recording for 30 days so that it can be downloaded or used to start a forked session. Stored sessions and their index expire after 30 days. Recording downloads and forking require a data policy that permits persistence and are not available with Zero Data Retention. Setting `store: false` on a fork prevents storage of the new session; it does not delete the source recording or remove the authorization required to read it. The API does not provide a public stored-session deletion endpoint. GPT-Live supports data residency in the United States and Europe. To achieve zero data retention, customers must take specific actions or avoid specific features within each of these areas: Prompt logging for abuse monitoring : As outlined in the Gemini API Additional Terms of Service , for Paid Services, Google logs prompts and responses for a limited period of time solely for detecting violations of the Prohibited Use Policy . When your request for ZDR for a particular project is approved, all user content (prompts and responses) and identifiable metadata (such as IP addresses and Google Account IDs) are cleared prior to logging. Interactions API : The Interactions API manages the active state of a conversation to enable multi-turn turns. By default, the Interactions API enables state storage . To ensure a zero-data footprint, you must explicitly set the store parameter to false in your API requests to opt out of the default state retention. Live API : This stateful API allows real-time reconnection by storing conversation state. To achieve zero data retention, do not configure SessionResumptionConfig . Distillation is a method used to extract the capabilities of advanced models. It is often employed on an industrial scale, using thousands of fake accounts. Distillation is a safety risk, since the distilled capabilities can subsequently be released without adequate safeguards. 1 comes with strengthened mechanisms to make distillation attacks harder. For example, it is no longer possible for new API accounts (those created from today onwards) to manually edit Claude’s prior context in a multi-turn conversation while preserving the transcript of Claude’s prior thinking.
